---
title: "How one ranking is made"
description: "A complete, synthetic walkthrough from one request to a frozen candidate ranking."
---

::: {.hub-example-notice}
## A teaching example, not experiment evidence

Everything below is fabricated: the request, candidate names, histories,
scores, and rankings. No private response text, candidate identity, or model
rationale appears here. The example explains the pipeline; it does not show
that any candidate has a real capability.
:::

## 1. Start with the request and objective

> “Explain why my balcony basil leaves are turning yellow, then give me a safe
> two-week recovery plan.”

The system must rank all 150 candidates for this request. To keep the diagram
readable, we follow three fictional candidates:

- **GardenGuide:** a label associated with practical plant guidance;
- **QuickFacts:** a label associated with concise factual explanations;
- **CodeTutor:** a label associated with programming help.

The output is an ordered list of candidates. The system is **not** writing the
basil answer, and a plausible candidate name is not proof of capability.

## 2. Draw the evidence boundary before scoring

::: {.hub-evidence-boundary}
**Allowed:** the new request; frozen candidate labels; released historical
development requests and their permitted judgments; and frozen summaries of
historical candidate responses.

**Forbidden:** the new request's own relevance judgment, hidden-test labels,
private raw responses in this guide, or any evidence collected after the
ranking is frozen.
:::

Historical development judgments can influence a method learned from similar
past requests. That makes the current promoted development system useful for
development research, but not wholly qrel-free. Building the unseen-query
pipeline in issue [#39](https://github.com/npatta01/trec_mlm_2026/issues/39)
is therefore a pre-test requirement.

## 3. Look for similar historical requests

Imagine the released development set contains requests about yellow herb
leaves, safe plant recovery, and unrelated software debugging. A dense
nearest-neighbor search compares their meanings with the basil request.

The method does not copy a past answer. It transfers the historical candidate
ranking signal from the closest requests. In this fabricated example it gives:

1. GardenGuide
2. QuickFacts
3. CodeTutor

This is the strongest current **query-side** reference signal.

## 4. Compare the request with candidate labels

Candidate labels provide another clue. “GardenGuide” overlaps the topic and
“CodeTutor” does not, so a label-only route could produce the same ordering.
But labels are descriptions, not verified capability records. This route is a
useful control, not the promoted development choice.

## 5. Summarize each candidate's historical responses

For each candidate, the semantic-profile method groups that candidate's past
response embeddings and stores compact centroids. A centroid is the numerical
center of a response group; an optional cluster name is only a human-readable
explanation and never changes the score.

For example, GardenGuide might have a fabricated profile region near “plant
diagnosis and staged recovery,” while CodeTutor's profile regions concern
software. The current request is compared with these summaries—never with a
hidden target answer.

This is the strongest current **candidate-history** signal. The completed E5
follow-up also tested a bounded candidate-local raw-response refinement, but it
remains off-ledger, unregistered, and unpromoted.

## 6. Keep the signal rankings separate

Before fusion, each route produces its own complete ranking. Here are three
fabricated top-three views:

| Evidence route | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | What the route means |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Similar historical requests | GardenGuide | QuickFacts | CodeTutor | Past request neighborhoods favor GardenGuide. |
| Candidate semantic profiles | QuickFacts | GardenGuide | CodeTutor | Candidate-history summaries slightly favor QuickFacts. |
| Candidate labels (control) | GardenGuide | QuickFacts | CodeTutor | Label text favors the plant-oriented name. |

These disagreements are useful. If the routes are collapsed too early, a
strong signal can be diluted by a weak one and the failure becomes harder to
diagnose.

## 7. Fuse the two frozen development signals

The promoted development system uses **equal reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF)**
for the dense similar-request ranking and the semantic-profile ranking. RRF
turns each rank position into a small score and adds the two scores; “equal”
means neither route receives a tuned advantage.

Using a small teaching constant so the arithmetic is visible:

| Candidate | Similar-request contribution | Profile contribution | Sum | Final rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GardenGuide | 1 / (3 + 1) = 0.250 | 1 / (3 + 2) = 0.200 | 0.450 | 1 |
| QuickFacts | 1 / (3 + 2) = 0.200 | 1 / (3 + 1) = 0.250 | 0.450 | 2¹ |
| CodeTutor | 1 / (3 + 3) = 0.167 | 1 / (3 + 3) = 0.167 | 0.334 | 3 |

¹The production implementation has a deterministic tie rule. This teaching
table preserves the invented ordering and is not a reproduction of a run.

The frozen illustrative result is therefore **GardenGuide → QuickFacts →
CodeTutor**. Candidate labels helped us understand the example but are not an
extra component in the promoted fusion.

## 8. Evaluate only after construction is complete

On the development set, legitimate qrels can evaluate the already-frozen
ordering using ranking metrics. The request's own qrel must not be read while
constructing that request's ranking. On the hidden test, no effectiveness
claim is available until the organizer releases evaluation evidence.

This separation answers two different questions:

- **Construction:** what evidence produced the ranking?
- **Evaluation:** after freezing it, how well did that ranking match judgments?

## 9. Diagnose the miss and name the next falsifier

If later development evaluation says QuickFacts should have ranked first, we
inspect the components rather than immediately inventing another mixture.

- If the profile ranked QuickFacts first but fusion moved it down, this is a
  **fusion-dilution** candidate: test a preregistered preservation gate.
- If neither component ranked QuickFacts well, fusion cannot recover a signal
  that is absent: improve the evidence source or stop.
- If generated comparison evidence was unreliable, first test its grounding;
  do not treat fluent text as a gold answer.

These are falsifiable branches, not post-hoc excuses. The
[failure-mechanism library](failure-library.qmd) gives the complete evidence
and stop-rule template.

## 10. State what this example cannot establish

This walkthrough does **not** establish that:

- the fabricated candidates correspond to real systems;
- the shown rankings or arithmetic came from an experiment;
- candidate labels, cluster names, or old responses prove capability;
- equal RRF will generalize to the hidden test;
- E5 refinement is registered or promoted; or
- selected failure cases measure how common a mechanism is.

For actual run facts, use the [ledger explorer](../evidence/runs.qmd), which is
generated from the exact experiment ledger.
For bounded conclusions, use the [study index](../studies/index.qmd).
